# Summary {#part-safety-summary .unnumbered}

Safety gathered questions that had been appearing at every boundary: what the model represents internally, how oversight scales, what permissions a tool call carries, how runtime policy is enforced, what happens under attack, what data is remembered, and what law or governance structure applies after harm. These are related questions, but they do not live at one layer.

That mismatch is the main source of false confidence. A policy sentence, a classifier, a permission boundary, a red-team report, and a legal duty each control a different object. A safety claim becomes credible only when its evidence, authority, enforcement point, and failure mode are located in the stack.

The takeaway is not to search for a single switch. It is to trace where control is asserted and where it can be tested. The open question is how governance should adapt as models gain more autonomy, tool access, and cross-border deployment while the technical evidence remains incomplete. Part IX moves below the policy surface to the physical and operational substrate: silicon, power, cluster failures, data limits, and frontier measurement decide what those controls can scale to.
